Primary study: Liu et al., *Schizophrenia Research* (2014), PMID 25445624. This two-stage Han Chinese case-control study included a Hunan discovery cohort (986 cases, 1,040 controls) and a Yunnan replication cohort (564 cases, 547 controls). The authors reported that the rs2301228-A promoter allele was associated with schizophrenia at the allelic level in discovery and validated in the replication cohort. They also reported that A reduced NCAM1 transcription in luciferase assays.

The retrieved abstract does **not** provide allele or genotype odds ratios, 95% confidence intervals, or exact p-values, so those numerical estimates cannot be reported from the available evidence. It describes allelic association; it does not establish a specific genotype effect in the retrieved record. Searches identified no separate rs2301228 schizophrenia replication or null case-control study; the Yunnan cohort is the reported replication within the primary study.

The evidence supports a positive association in the reported Han Chinese study, with within-study replication and a functional reporter assay; the retrieved abstract lacks effect-size statistics, so I will avoid overstating magnitude. I’ll record the primary finding and source provenance in the evidence graph.

Yes. The primary study by Liu et al. reported that the **A allele of NCAM1 promoter variant rs2301228** was significantly associated with schizophrenia in Han Chinese participants. The association was found in a Hunan discovery cohort (986 cases, 1,040 controls) and validated in a Yunnan replication cohort (564 cases, 547 controls). In luciferase assays, the A allele also significantly reduced NCAM1 transcription.

The evidence supports the allele as a reported risk marker in those cohorts, but the retrieved abstract did not provide odds ratios, confidence intervals, or exact p-values. The validation was within the same two-stage study; the available search results did not identify an independent external replication.

Source: Liu et al., *Schizophrenia Research* (2014), PMID 25445624.

FINAL DECISION: YES
